content: The Greek citron, scientifically referred to as Citrus Medica variety etrog, is primarily associated with its use in Jewish rituals during the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot). Historically, this variety was predominantly cultivated on the island of Corfu. However, no citron trees remain on Corfu today. Currently, this variety is the most prominent in Israel, where it is highly sought after for religious purposes due to its natural aesthetic appeal, including its typically persistent style and stigma. While the Greek citron can still be found on some Greek islands, such as Crete and Naxos, where it is used to produce specialty liqueurs, its cultivation for ritual purposes is now largely confined to Israel. The Greek citron became significant for the Ashkenazic Jewish community during the Napoleonic Wars, when the importation of the Yanova citron was disrupted due to the ongoing battles. The introduction of this new citron variety raised concerns for decades, particularly regarding the possibility of grafting or hybridization. Rabbi Efraim Zalman Margalioth, in his responsa Beis Efraim (volume 1, section 56), confirmed during his time that no grafted citron trees were present on Corfu. This certification, along with the more lenient rulings of other rabbinic authorities, eventually led to the acceptance of the Corfu citron (Esrog) for ritual use. As the Greek citron market expanded, citrons were also imported from other regions of Greece, including Parga, Rapiza, and Agia. However, disputes arose over whether these plantations maintained the same level of kashrut as those on Corfu. Around 1850, Sir Moses Montefiore initiated efforts to establish citron plantations in Israel to support Jewish settlers facing hunger and hardship. The native Palestinian variety, known as the Beladdi, was considered inferior in terms of shape, color, and other characteristics, including its lack of a persistent style. Sephardic Jewish settlers, who had traditionally been lenient regarding the Corfu citron, planted seeds in Israel's coastal regions, particularly near Jaffa. Over time, Arab farmers imported cuttings from Greece and grafted them onto lemon rootstock. The Corfu variety, referred to locally as Kabbud abu Nunia (the citron with a persistent style), faced challenges adapting to the Palestinian climate, leading to widespread grafting practices. Sephardic rabbis, along with some Ashkenazic authorities, permitted the use of Jaffa citrons after inspecting each fruit individually prior to harvest. However, the leading Ashkenazic rabbinic authorities in Jerusalem only approved the Beladdi variety, which was primarily cultivated in areas such as Safed, Shechem (Nablus), and the Arab village of Umm al-Fahm. Plantations near Tiberias were also deemed acceptable. According to the Hebrew writer Osof Gur, in his work Toldos Hoesrog Beretz Yisroel, the Beladdi variety is characterized by a crisp texture and a slightly sweet inner rind, while its pulp is notably high in acidity.
